title: The basket in the reeds (Exodus 2:1–10)
hookLine: a mother, a sister watching, a princess who pities a crying baby

cards: When the midwives won't do it, Pharaoh stops pretending. He orders all his people: every son born to the Hebrews, throw him into the river. Into this, a baby boy is born to a family from the tribe of Levi.

His mother sees, the text says, that he is a goodly child, and she hides him for three months. Three months of a newborn, hidden: the crying, the night feedings, the neighbors. Then he gets too big and too loud to hide.

teach.b: So she does something brave and strange.
In the King James Bible: "she took for him an ark of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime and with pitch, and put the child therein; and she laid it in the flags by the river's brink." An ark.
The Hebrew word is tevah, the same word Genesis uses for Noah's ark: once a boat that carried the whole world through the flood, now a little one, sealed with tar, carrying one baby.
She puts him in the very river Pharaoh wanted him thrown into.
"And his sister stood afar off, to wit what would be done to him." Someone was watching. Then Pharaoh's daughter comes down to bathe.

teach.h: THE BABE WEPT. SHE HAD COMPASSION.
teach.b: She has the basket brought and opens it, "and, behold, the babe wept. And she had compassion on him." She knows he's one of the Hebrews' children, and she keeps him anyway, against her own father's order.
Now the sister moves: shall I find a Hebrew woman to nurse him for you? Go, says the princess. So the sister brings back the baby's own mother, who is paid to nurse her own son.

teach.h: BECAUSE I DREW HIM OUT OF THE WATER.
teach.b: When he's older, the princess adopts him and names him: "Because I drew him out of the water." Moses. Look at who saves him: a mother, a sister, a foreign princess, and before them, two midwives.
Not one of them is a king or a soldier, and the one with royal blood is defying her own father. Every one of them was paying attention.
Some Christian readers notice another baby, in Matthew's Gospel, whose life was threatened by a king, carried to safety in Egypt.

how: Christians tell the story of baby Moses to children, and some read it alongside Matthew 2, where the infant Jesus escapes King Herod; churches use it to speak about protecting children and welcoming adopted and foster children.

practice: Think of someone small in your life: a child, a grandchild, a neighbor's kid, or someone small in another way, a person easily overlooked.
Picture yourself like the sister, standing a little way off, watching to see what will happen to them, ready to step in. If you pray, you can pray for them by name; if not, simply hold them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Tevah. Hebrew for ark, the same word for Noah's: the little basket of bulrushes where a mother hid her baby in the Nile.
